newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Hypo-Bank raises stake in F&C.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hypo-Bank raises stake in F&C.

text.p: Germany's Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel- Bank AG said on Thursday it planned to raise its stake in British fund manager Foreign & Colonial Management and would use the firm as a base for acquisition-led growth.

The bank also concluded the reporting season of nine-month bank earnings by posting a 9.9 percent rise in operating profit to 808.1 million marks, falling well short of analysts' expectations and lagging profits growth at its major rivals.
Hypo-Bank said it aimed to increase its stake in F&C to 65 percent from 50 percent for a price of 60 million pounds and hoped to seal the purchase this year.
Consolidating F&C would boost Hypo-Bank's net commission income by between 140 and 170 million marks, the bank said.

"We plan to conduct our international expansion in fund management via Foreign & Colonial," Hypo-Bank management board member Martin Koelsch told a news conference. "The intention is clear - we are not just aiming at organic growth but also at broadening that business through acquisitions."

Hypo-Bank's move fits a trend by German banks to buy fund management firms in Britain and the U.S. with the aim of growing in a business seen as providing safe, steady returns while not binding too much capital.
Only last week, Dresdner Bank AG said it planned to merge its foreign institutional funds business under one roof, pushing forward its aim to become a global player in asset management.
Koelsch said Hypo-Bank was not in talks about acquisitions at present and had no plans to raise its stake in F&C further.

Hypo-Bank said it was impressed by F&C's increasing profitability and its growth in funds under management to 26.9 billion pounds. F&C is among the top six institutional fund managers in Britain and is a market leader for emerging markets funds in Europe, Hypo-Bank said.
Koelsch said Hypo-Bank had no plans to buy a stake in U.S. asset management firm Massachusetts Finanacial Services (MFS) which entered into a strategic alliance with F&C last year.
Separately, Hypo-Bank reported earnings which fell far short of analysts' forecasts, partly because of a 20 percent rise in net risk provisions to 961 million marks.
Chief executive Eberhard Martini said he saw "no light at the end of the tunnel" for provisions as risks remained high.
The bank, a strong mortgage lender, said net interest income rose 8.3 percent to 3.4 billion marks while net commission income rose 7.8 percent to 662.5 million marks.
Own-account trading profit rose a modest 6.5 percent to 130.3 million marks, a sharp improvement after a 35.4 percent decline in the first six months.
Administration costs grew just 0.9 percent to 1.88 billion marks, well below cost growth at Hypo-Bank's larger rivals.
Martini said the bank would pay an unchanged dividend of 1.45 marks per share for 1996 and said the bank would most probably not need to raise capital next year.

Despite the disappointing earnings, Hypo-Bank's shares closed up 0.35 marks or 0.7 percent at 47.35 marks. Dealers said German bank shares in general were driven by a renewed outburst of merger speculation.
Martini was more frank on the issue of mergers than executives at rival banks. He said most bankers had mulled the possibility that merger activity may break out in their sector.

"Every banker has thought over all possibilities," Martini said. "It could well be that the current market speculation about mergers will blow over. But we as managers must be prepared for all eventualities."
But Hypo-Bank was confident of staying independent, he added.
